Sookti Retail Systems: One Page, Four Headings

A product director has until seven on Monday morning to settle a problem, a proposal, a why-now and a list of what she will not build — on one page, read cold.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At 22:40 on Sunday 15 November 2026, Deepashikha Kodoth had Draft B of her one-pager open at the dining table of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with Draft A face-down beside it. The two pages did not say the same thing. Draft A (Exhibit 2), circulated on Friday 2 October, put the problem at ₹4.36 crore a year and proposed rebuilding the matching engine. Draft B (Exhibit 6), written on Wednesday 11 November, put it at ₹143.28 lakh a year and proposed something narrower. Between them sat the September close, a Toronto re-analysis and her chief technology officer's capacity note.

By 07:00 one of the two — or a third page she had not written — had to be in the Build Council pack. The Council would sit from 10:00 to 12:30 IST with nine proposals and five minutes each, and would see no appendix, because under Sookti's operating charter there is none. What it would see was one page: problem, proposal, why now, what we are not doing.

2. Sookti, and the decision that still binds it

Sookti Retail Systems Private Limited was founded in Bengaluru in February 2019 to sell store-operations software to Indian retail chains, in the territory GoFrugal, Ginesys, Unicommerce and Increff also work. It closed FY26 at ₹161 crore of revenue and carried ₹178 crore of annual recurring revenue at 30 September 2026, across 214 chains and 640 staff in Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, New Jersey and Dubai. Sookti Store runs the shop floor; Sookti Ledger reconciles what each of 11,480 stores is owed across payment and marketplace channels.

The decision that still shapes every funding request was taken in March 2023. In November 2022 the board had approved a 41-page requirements document for Ledger; the module shipped nine months late, and the post-mortem found three of its core assumptions contradicted inside the document itself. The founders' answer was the One Page Rule: one A4 page at 11 point, 420 words maximum, four fixed headings, no appendix, no attachments. The Build Council reads cold and decides in the room, and no multi-page specification has been approved since.

3. The industry around the ledger

Indian retail settlement has become a many-to-many problem in six years. A chain that once reconciled cash and two card acquirers now reconciles UPI across NPCI's rails, cards under the Reserve Bank of India's card-on-file tokenisation regime, wallets, gift instruments, and payouts from Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Swiggy and Zomato, each remitting on its own cycle, in its own format, net of its own deductions, and all of them at festival volumes through Onam and Diwali. ONDC has added counterparties again. GST e-invoicing adds a second ledger that must agree with the first, and GSTN's API migration carries a hard date of 1 April 2027. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the customer telephone numbers inside most payout files mean every new adapter needs a data-processing addendum.

The exposure is not only Indian. Suvega Hypermarts, 412 stores out of Hyderabad, pays ₹3.60 crore a year. Suhool Markets LLC of Dubai, 162 stores across the UAE and Oman, signed a three-year contract in July 2025 worth ₹14.40 crore, or ₹4.80 crore a year — Sookti's largest single contract by annual value. Suhool reconciles against UAE marketplace partners under 5 per cent VAT, on formats nobody in Bengaluru had seen before 2025.

4. The situation in detail

18 March 2026. A Pune engineering review sampled 1,400 unmatched settlement lines from the February 2026 close. In 854 of the 1,400 — 61.0 per cent — the store's day-close timestamp fell after the channel's settlement cut-off. It concluded that unmatched lines were a store-discipline problem spread roughly in proportion to channel volume; the FY27 planning assumption followed.

7 September 2026. The August close ran: 22,418 lines did not match, and 8,640 escalated to Sookti's settlement support pod in Pune; Exhibit 4 prices what the rest cost the chains.

7 October 2026. The September close ran, five days after Draft A went out: 24,094 lines did not match, 7.7 per cent above the FY26 monthly average of 22,367, and 9,120 escalated. Exhibit 1 is that close by channel, and Exhibit 3 prices the escalations. The October close had not been signed off when Draft B was written.

28 October 2026. Devaprasad Kavoor, in Toronto, re-ran the March sample and the September population. From the same February close he drew a control of 1,400 matched lines: 812 of the 1,400 controls, 58.0 per cent, carried the same late day-close pattern — 3.0 points of difference against a standard error of 1.9 points. On the September population, marketplace payouts were 11.70 per cent of all settlement lines and 47.21 per cent of all unmatched lines; and counting files rather than lines, the 11,374 unmatched marketplace lines arrived in 318 payout files, 41 of which produced 7,906 of the lines.

5. The people

Deepashikha Kodoth, Director of Product, Settlement & Ledger, Bengaluru, owns the page. Her 11 November position is deterministic matching for the five Indian marketplace formats; two of her last three one-pagers were declined. She has not told the Council that Draft A's ₹4.36 crore was not her calculation.

Dinanath Kottarathil, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, chairs the Council and wrote the 4 November capacity note. The One Page Rule is not negotiable, he says, and nor is the GSTN date, which is his exposure to the board. He has not said that he has already told the Council's other two members he will not fund a rebuild this quarter.

Dipayan Karkada, engineering manager of the nine-person Ledger squad, Pune, wrote the 2021 matcher and produced all four estimates on 21 October. Patching formats one at a time, he argues, is how the matcher reached this state, so fund the rebuild. He has not said that two of the five Indian partners changed their payout schema late that month.

Dhrituja Kemmannu, senior product designer, Berlin, holds that the line count is the wrong target and that a bulk console would cut the minutes a human spends per line whatever the count does. The console is her design, carried into three Councils. She has not said that its usability study ran with nine participants, seven from one chain.

Devaprasad Kavoor, senior data scientist, Toronto, wrote the 28 October re-analysis, which is his case for a staff promotion. Both drafts count the wrong unit, he says, because the fault arrives as a file and not a line. He has not said that one chain, Suvega Hypermarts, accounts for 38 per cent of the unmatched marketplace lines in his figure.

Duleep Kolathur, head of customer success for APAC, Singapore, carries Suhool's renewal in his number. Clause 11.4 attaches a contractual date to the UAE formats and nothing else, he argues, so they go first. He has not said that Suhool's finance head told him in October that Suhool has never invoked the clause on any vendor.

Debangshu Kaippally, regional vice-president for sales, North America, New Jersey, is building a US pipeline in which "channel settlement matching" is a procurement checklist item, and wants the largest version of the problem on the page. He gave Kodoth the ₹4.36 crore by telephone on Tuesday 29 September 2026, and has not said that he reached it by adding two pools paid from different pockets.

8. The options as Kodoth sees them on Sunday night

A, Marketplace Match. Deterministic matching for the five Indian partner formats: 46 engineer-weeks, ₹24.84 lakh of build, 3,892 of September's escalated lines. It leaves the 2021 matcher and the two UAE formats where they are.

B, Clearing Console. Bulk clearing for client finance teams and the Pune pod: 24 engineer-weeks, ₹12.96 lakh. It moves no line out of the unmatched column, taking handling from eleven minutes to seven on all 9,120 escalations.

C, Ledger Rebuild. A new engine across all channels: 58 engineer-weeks, the whole free budget, ₹31.32 lakh, and ₹6.80 lakh a year off the carry when the Mumbai cluster goes. It lands on 11 March 2027, the window's last buildable day, with the freeze immediately after.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The page must be in the Council pack by 07:00 IST on Monday 16 November 2026, and the Council decides in the room.

Capacity is the 58 free engineer-weeks of Exhibit 5, over the ten buildable weeks of 1 January to 11 March 2027; the GSTN migration takes 22 of the gross 90 and falls due 1 April 2027. The change freeze runs 12 to 31 March for clients' year-end close. The FY27 budget holds Ledger headcount at nine until 1 April 2027, so nothing can be bought with money instead of weeks.

Clause 11.4 permits Suhool to withhold 15 per cent of its ₹4.80 crore annual fee, or ₹72 lakh, if UAE marketplace matching is not delivered by 31 March 2027. Under the DPDP Act, 2023, each new partner adapter needs a data-processing addendum, and legal review runs three weeks inside the ten.

  3. Draft A and Draft B state different problems. Using Figure 2, separate what changed in the evidence between 2 October and 11 November from what changed in Kodoth's reading of it.
  4. The charter allows one page and no appendix. Take Exhibits 1, 3, 4 and 5 in turn: what must each lose to fit, and who carries the risk of the remainder?
  5. Exhibit 5 puts a one-off build cost, an annual carrying change and a one-month support effect in one table. Price A with D against C over the first twelve months after delivery, listing the assumptions you supply.
  6. Kavoor counts the 11,374 unmatched marketplace lines as 318 payout files; Draft B counts lines. If the unit on the problem line changes, what else must change with it? And at 07:00 on Monday 16 November, what page does Kodoth put in the pack, and what does she say to the board in February if that problem line was the wrong figure?

11. Sunday night, continued

At 23:30 Kodoth read Draft A's problem line again — ₹4.36 crore, typed in October from a telephone call — and then Draft B's last three lines, the ones that say what Sookti will not be doing.

Kolathur's email was open in a third window. Karkada's estimates were dated 21 October. The GSTN migration would take its 22 engineer-weeks whatever the page said. She had 420 words, four headings and seven and a half hours, and had not yet decided which problem Sookti had.

Writing a one-pager

Problem, proposal, why now, what we are not doing — and why the hardest word on the page is the one you delete.

1Eight minutes in Lower Parel

At 7:40 on the morning of Thursday, 12 February 2026, Rohit Bhandari sat in an empty meeting room on the fourth floor of Shehnai Money's office in Lower Parel, Mumbai, with three printed pages in front of him and a red pen he had not yet uncapped. Shehnai Money is a consumer investing application: 4.1 million registered users, 1.62 million of whom hold at least one active systematic investment plan, or SIP — a standing instruction that debits a fixed amount from the user's bank account on a fixed date each month and buys mutual fund units with it. The company earns almost nothing on each transaction; it earns a small annual trail on the assets it holds, which means its economics are entirely a function of how long money stays and how reliably it arrives.

At eleven that morning, the quarterly planning committee would meet. Eight proposals had been submitted; the engineering capacity available was, by the CTO's arithmetic, enough for three. Each product manager had been given the same allowance: one page, circulated twenty-four hours in advance, and six minutes of discussion. Rohit had written three pages. He knew, in the way one knows these things at 7:40 in the morning, that they were three pages of hedging.

His proposal had a working title, "SIP Rescue," and a real idea underneath it. Every month a substantial number of SIP instalments failed on the debit date — insufficient balance, an expired mandate, a bank-side error. Most recovered. Some did not, and the ones that did not appeared, in the cohort charts Rohit had been staring at since November, to be the leading edge of something worse: users who stopped investing altogether and, some months later, stopped opening the app. If he lost the argument, the four engineers he wanted would go instead to a redesign of the wealth-summary screen, and the failure cohort would keep compounding for another quarter. If he won it on bad reasoning — if he inflated the number and the committee later discovered it — he would spend the next year being read sceptically, which in a company that decides by document is a slower and more permanent kind of loss.

The committee's chair was Farida Qureshi, the VP of Product, who had been at Shehnai Money for five years and had a single rule she repeated so often that new joiners quoted it before they understood it: if I cannot tell from the page what we are not doing, I assume you have not decided anything.

2What a one-pager actually is

A one-pager is a written argument, typically four hundred to seven hundred words, that asks a named person to make a single decision, and that makes the case by establishing four things: the problem, stated as measured evidence rather than as an adjective; the proposal, stated as a change in what somebody will be able to do; why now, meaning what it is about this quarter rather than any other that makes the work timely; and what we are not doing, meaning the scope a reasonable reader would otherwise assume was included and which you are explicitly declining. It is a decision document. It is not a description document, and the distinction matters more than any question of format.

The artefact has a long commercial lineage. Procter & Gamble is usually credited with institutionalising the one-page memo in the 1930s under Richard Deupree, who is said to have returned longer documents unread; the discipline survived there for decades as a hiring and promotion filter as much as a communication standard. Barbara Minto, working at McKinsey in the 1960s and 1970s, gave the underlying logic its most durable formulation in what became the Pyramid Principle: state the answer first, then the small number of independent reasons that support it, then the evidence beneath each reason. Amazon pushed the idea furthest in the other direction from about 2004, when Jeff Bezos replaced slide presentations with narrative memos read silently at the start of the meeting, and paired the practice with the PR/FAQ, a document written as though the product had already launched. In product management, the one-pager settled into its modern role sometime in the 2010s as the artefact that comes before the product requirements document — the thing you write to establish that the PRD is worth writing.

The problem all of these were invented to solve is the same one Rohit faced at 7:40 that morning. The cost of a decision meeting rises steeply with how much thinking has to be done inside the room. A room of eight senior people doing first-pass thinking together is the most expensive way yet devised to reach a mediocre conclusion, because the loudest framing arrives first and the group spends its time reacting to it. Writing moves the thinking to before the room, where it is cheap, private, and subject to revision. The page limit is not an aesthetic preference. It is a forcing function on selection: when only six hundred words fit, the author must decide which facts are load-bearing, and that act of deciding is the actual work.

The sentence Rohit could have said in the meeting without sounding glib was this one: a one-pager is not a short PRD; it is the argument that we should write the PRD at all.

3The mechanics, including the steps nobody mentions

Practitioners describe writing a one-pager as though it were four paragraphs written in order. In practice it is seven steps, three of which are almost never stated.

The first unstated step is to name the decision and the decider. Rohit's three pages nowhere said what he wanted. They described a phenomenon. Before writing a word he should have written, for himself, a sentence of the form: I am asking Farida to allocate four engineers for one quarter beginning 1 March, and I need the answer by 12 February because the sprint boundary is the 16th. A page written to nobody in particular ends up addressed to everybody, which in practice means it is addressed to the author's own anxiety.

The second step is to state the problem as a measured quantity. "SIP failures are hurting retention" is an adjective wearing a business suit. The measured version needs a numerator, a denominator, a date range and a source: of 1.62 million active mandates, 138,000 instalments failed on their debit date in January 2026, and 41,000 of those had not resumed within ninety days.

The third step is to state the proposal as a change in behaviour. Not "build a retry orchestration service and a notification pipeline," which describes the inside of the machine, but "a user whose SIP is about to fail is warned two days before the debit, and a user whose SIP has already failed can restore it in two taps from the home screen rather than through the mandate settings flow." Engineers will translate that into services; the committee cannot.

The fourth step is why now, and it admits only three honest forms. A window that closes: a regulatory date, a partner integration, a competitor's move, a seasonal peak. A cost that compounds: the problem is not merely present but accumulating, so that waiting a quarter costs more than a quarter. A dependency that has just landed: some other team has finished something that makes this cheap for the first time. The dishonest form — the one that appears most often — is "this has been on the backlog for a long time," which is a fact about the backlog rather than about the world.

The fifth step is the non-goals, and the useful test is social rather than logical: each non-goal should make at least one identifiable colleague mildly unhappy. A non-goal nobody minds is not a decision, it is a decoration. "We are not building a credit line to cover failed debits" mattered at Shehnai Money precisely because the growth team had been asking for exactly that for two quarters.

The sixth step is the cost and the check: roughly what the bet costs, and what evidence, by what date, would show it working or failing. The seventh — the one that separates people who write one-pagers from people who have heard of them — is the cut. You write fourteen hundred words and then remove eight hundred. Deciding what to delete is not tidying up after the thinking; it is the thinking, because every deletion is a judgement that a particular fact is not load-bearing.

4The arithmetic, done twice

Rohit's first draft opened with a number he was proud of. Of 1.62 million active mandates, 138,000 instalments failed in January. At an average instalment of ₹2,900, that is 138,000 × ₹2,900 = ₹40.0 crore of monthly inflow disrupted, which annualises to roughly ₹480 crore. The sentence he had written was: ₹480 crore of annual investment inflow is at risk from SIP failure.

It is a thrilling sentence and it does not survive one round of division. Of the 138,000 failures, 97,000 recovered within the same month — either through the automatic retry that the mandate framework permits, or because the user topped up the account after the failure notification. Only 41,000 lapsed, meaning they had not resumed ninety days later. The honest inflow figure is therefore 41,000 × ₹2,900 = ₹11.9 crore of monthly recurring inflow lost, from each month's fresh cohort.

Now convert inflow into revenue, which is where most first drafts quietly stop. Shehnai Money earns a trail of roughly 0.35% per annum on assets under management. A monthly inflow stream of ₹11.9 crore does not produce ₹11.9 crore of assets on day one; it accumulates, so the average balance across the first year is roughly half the annual total. The annual inflow is ₹11.9 crore × 12 = ₹142.8 crore; the average balance is about ₹71 crore; the trail is 0.35% × ₹71 crore = ₹25 lakh in the first year. If the feature recovered 35% of lapses, the revenue recovered in year one would be 0.35 × ₹25 lakh = ₹8.7 lakh. Against four engineers for a quarter — twelve engineer-months at a fully loaded ₹5 lakh a month, or ₹60 lakh — the proposal loses, badly, on the argument Rohit had been planning to make.

The case is real, but it is carried by something else. Rohit's cohort analysis showed that a user whose SIP lapses has a 22% probability of leaving the app within six months, against a base rate of 6.5% for otherwise comparable users — an incremental 15.5 percentage points. Applied to 41,000 lapses a month, that is 6,355 users lost per month who would otherwise have stayed. At a lifetime value of ₹4,100 per retained user, the monthly cost is 6,355 × ₹4,100 = ₹2.6 crore, or roughly ₹31 crore a year. Recovering 35% of it is ₹10.9 crore a year against ₹60 lakh of engineering. That argument wins, and it wins by a factor of eighteen.

Lifetime value of ₹4,100 is the finance team's 2025 blended figure for a user with at least one active SIP. Churn rates are from a matched cohort of 18,400 users, October 2024 to September 2025.

Now change one input, which is what a committee will do the moment the page is read carefully. The 15.5-point churn delta is a correlation. It is entirely possible that lapsing does not cause departure but merely reveals a user who was already disengaging — the job loss, the household cash crunch, the decision to move money to a different provider. Suppose, conservatively, that only half the churn delta is actually caused by the lapse and is therefore addressable. The annual cost falls from ₹31 crore to ₹15.5 crore; recovering 35% of it yields ₹5.4 crore against ₹60 lakh of cost. The proposal still wins, by a factor of nine.

That second pass is the single most valuable paragraph Rohit can write, and it takes forty words on the page: if only half this churn is caused rather than revealed by the lapse, the case still returns nine times its cost; we would have to be wrong by roughly 9× for this to be a bad use of the quarter. A one-pager that names the assumption it is most likely to be wrong about, and shows the decision surviving that assumption breaking, has done something a longer document rarely manages.

5The nuances that separate understanding from vocabulary

A one-pager is not a short PRD

They answer different questions. The one-pager answers should we do this at all, now, instead of the alternatives; the product requirements document answers what exactly are we building, for whom, with what behaviour at the edges. The first is addressed to a decider and is thrown away once the decision is made; the second is addressed to a delivery team and lives as long as the feature does. People who compress a PRD into a page produce a document full of acceptance criteria and empty of argument, and they are surprised when the committee asks, "but why this quarter?"

The page limit is a selection constraint, not a formatting rule

The tell is font size. A page in nine-point type with half-centimetre margins has satisfied the letter of the constraint and evaded the whole point of it, which is to force the author to decide what matters. Farida Qureshi's practical countermeasure at Shehnai Money was to specify a word count rather than a page: six hundred words, and appendices permitted but explicitly optional reading.

“Why now” is a claim about the world, not about your enthusiasm

Because it is a claim about the world, it can be wrong, and a good reader will test it. "Our reconciliation service shipped in December, so the mandate-status feed we need is finally available in near real time" is a testable claim someone can verify in ten minutes. "The team is excited about this" is not a claim at all.

Non-goals only count if they cost something

The purpose of the not-doing section is to pre-commit against the scope creep that will otherwise arrive in week four, when a senior person asks an innocent question in a corridor. If the section lists only things nobody wanted, it buys no protection. The useful non-goals are the ones that felt slightly rude to write down.

Numbers are load-bearing, so they must survive division

The characteristic failure is the large round undivided number — ₹480 crore — which impresses on first reading and destroys the author's credibility on second. The discipline is simple: for every number on the page, be able to state its denominator, its date range and its source, and be willing to do so out loud without looking anything up.

The page must be falsifiable

A one-pager is a record of a decision made under uncertainty, which means it should name what would count as being wrong. "By 30 June, the proportion of lapsed SIPs that resume within thirty days rises from 11% to 25%, or we stop" converts an argument into an experiment with a stopping rule. Without it, the project can only end by exhaustion.

What it cannot tell you, however well written

It cannot tell you whether the thing is technically feasible, how long it will really take, or whether your organisation can execute it — those questions belong to design review, estimation, and honest history respectively. It is also not evidence of user need; it is an argument built on evidence gathered elsewhere. A beautifully written page resting on eleven interviews the author selected to agree with him is still a beautifully written page resting on eleven selected interviews.

The questions a newcomer should ask before relying on it

Three, in this order. Who is the decider, and have they agreed that this page is how the decision gets made? What decision is being asked for, in one sentence, and what is the deadline? And, asked of the author: what would change your mind? An author who cannot answer the third question has written advocacy, not analysis, and the difference will surface later at a worse moment.

6Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and small versus large

The four sections are stable across product types; what changes is which section is hardest, and it changes predictably.

In consumer products such as Shehnai Money, the problem section is comparatively easy because behavioural data is abundant — funnels, cohorts, session logs. The characteristic risk is the opposite one: abundant data makes it easy to dress an intuition in a chart and call it evidence. The discipline there is the second pass shown above, dividing the headline number until it becomes a revenue or retention figure that finance would recognise.

In business-to-business software the problem section is harder, because the person who feels the pain is rarely the person who signs the contract. Shailaja Health Cloud, a Chennai company selling laboratory information systems to 210 diagnostic-lab chains, learned this when a proposal to rebuild the phlebotomist's sample-collection app was rejected twice: the pain was real and was felt by staff who had no budget authority, and the page never connected it to anything the lab owner cared about, which was turnaround time and rejected-sample rates. The B2B "why now" is also different in kind — it is frequently a renewal date, an enterprise customer's procurement cycle, or a compliance deadline such as an integration milestone under the national digital health framework. And the non-goals are socially expensive, because writing "we are not building the custom report format that our third-largest customer asked for" means somebody in sales will read it.

In marketplaces, the problem statement must specify a side, and the non-goals must specify the side you are declining to help this quarter. Shailendra Freight Systems, a Pune platform matching truck capacity to shippers, found that its one-pagers were routinely ambiguous about whether a load-visibility improvement was for fleet owners or for consignors, with the consequence that the same document was read as two different proposals by two different vice-presidents. Marketplace pages also have to address the balance effect explicitly: any improvement that raises supply-side liquidity without demand to absorb it can make the experience worse for the side you were trying to help.

Company stage changes the job the document does. In a twelve-person company the one-pager is usually addressed to a founder who is physically present, and its real function is to slow down a decision that would otherwise be made in a corridor in ninety seconds. In a four-thousand-person company the function inverts: the page must travel without its author, surviving being read at 11 p.m. by a finance director three levels away who has never met the team. That reader needs the denominator, the date range and the source, because they cannot lean over and ask.

7Four common mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

The status update wearing the costume of a proposal. The symptom is a reader who finishes the page and asks, "so what do you want?" The underlying misunderstanding is that describing a situation thoroughly constitutes asking for something. The cheapest diagnostic is to hand the page to a colleague and ask them to circle the sentence containing the request; if they hesitate, or circle a heading, the sentence does not exist.

The everything-proposal. The symptom is that nobody objects in the meeting, which feels like success and is not; estimates then balloon in week three as scope arrives from every direction. The misunderstanding is that leaving options open is prudent, when in a planning committee it merely transfers the decision to whoever asks the most persistent question later. The diagnostic is to ask, at the end of the meeting, "what did we just decide not to do?" and to count how many people can answer.

The decorated number. The symptom is a figure that is large, round and undivided — ₹480 crore at risk — usually appearing in the first two sentences. The misunderstanding is that a number's job is to establish importance, when in fact its job is to establish magnitude relative to the cost of the fix. The diagnostic takes eight seconds: ask for the denominator and the date range.

The pre-read nobody read. The symptom is that the meeting opens with the author verbally summarising the document. The misunderstanding is that circulating a document is the same as it being read. Amazon's answer — silent reading for the first ten minutes of the meeting — is unfashionable and extremely effective; a lighter diagnostic is to count the comments that landed before the meeting, which at Shehnai Money averaged eleven for proposals that were eventually approved and two for those that were not.

8What good looks like

Here is the same decision handled well. Farida opens a 620-word document on the Wednesday evening. The first paragraph tells her that 41,000 SIP mandates lapsed in January out of 1.62 million active, that lapsing is associated with a 15.5-point increase in six-month churn, and that this costs roughly ₹31 crore a year in lifetime value, of which perhaps half is causally addressable. The second paragraph tells her what will change for a user: a warning two days before a debit that is likely to fail, and a two-tap restore path. The third tells her why this quarter: the mandate-status feed became available in near real time when the reconciliation service shipped in December, and each month of delay adds a fresh cohort of 41,000. The fourth tells her what is excluded: no credit line, no general-purpose retry engine, no change to the mandate-amount limits. The fifth names the cost, four engineers for a quarter, and the check: lapse-to-resume within thirty days must move from 11% to 25% by 30 June.

She reads it in four minutes and writes one comment: Is the 35% rescue assumption from a comparable product or from hope? That is what a good one-pager achieves. The meeting does not spend its six minutes establishing what the proposal is. It spends them on the single assumption that actually determines whether the decision is right.

9What Rohit did

At 9:15 he stopped editing the three pages and started again on a blank document, which is almost always faster than cutting. He led with churn rather than trail revenue, because the trail arithmetic — ₹8.7 lakh recovered against ₹60 lakh spent — would have sunk him, and because hiding it would have been worse than leading with the honest case. He wrote the causal caveat into the page rather than waiting to be asked. He wrote three non-goals, each of which he knew would irritate someone, and he wrote the stopping rule with a date on it. The finished document was 640 words with a two-page appendix marked optional.

The committee gave him three engineers rather than four, with a checkpoint at six weeks — a smaller yes than he wanted, and a yes he could defend, which is the better of the two outcomes when the assumption underneath is still unproven. Farida's note in the minutes was four words long: good page, thin assumption.

What to learn next follows directly. Writing clearly is the skill this artefact rests on: a one-pager is unforgiving of vague sentences because there are so few of them, and the habits that make a sentence carry weight — concrete subjects, active verbs, one idea per sentence — are learnable independently of any template. After that, PRD structure, because a one-pager that wins buys you the right to write the document that follows, and the two artefacts fail in opposite directions: a one-pager fails by being too long, a PRD by being too vague about the edges.

Two questions to sit with. First: in the last proposal you wrote, what was the largest number on the page, and could you state its denominator, its date range and its source without looking them up? Second: what is the one assumption you are most likely to be wrong about, and would your reader know from the page that you had noticed it?

Shehnai Money, Shailaja Health Cloud and Shailendra Freight Systems are fictional composites used for teaching. Market institutions, regulatory frameworks and mandate mechanics referred to as context are real; no conduct is attributed to any real firm.
case20v1-req.one.pager:
Ritham Fleet Cloud: One Page for the Committee

A teaching case on writing a one-pager

1. Opening

On Thursday 22 October 2026, Chinju Jayasankar, a senior product manager at Ritham Fleet Cloud, opened her thirteen-page requirements draft in the Kochi office. Her proposal, a toll-claims feature for fleet customers, would go before the quarterly planning committee at 10:00 IST on Tuesday 3 November. Pre-reads were due by 17:00 on Friday 30 October, eight days away. The committee would fund one seven-engineer squad for the quarter beginning 16 November. She had to decide what to send: the full draft, a single page, or no document at all.

2. Company background

Ritham was founded in Kochi in 2017 and sells fleet-management software to road-freight operators: trip tracking, a driver app, and ledgers for fuel and toll cost. It has 410 fleet customers running roughly 31,000 trucks, annual recurring revenue of ₹52 crore, and about 140 staff in Kochi, Pune and Bengaluru. Revenue works out at about ₹1,400 per truck per month. The company began with Kerala operators, spread to Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra after 2020, and now sells mainly to fleets of 40 to 200 trucks whose owners still run accounts through a clerk and a spreadsheet. A contract design studio works from Berlin, customer success is led from Singapore, and a sales head in Edison, New Jersey, handles global accounts.

The competition is crowded. Tata Motors and Mahindra bundle telematics with trucks, and BlackBuck sells trip services and FASTag to the same truckers. Tolls move through FASTag on NPCI's National Electronic Toll Collection system at NHAI plazas, and the issuing banks, not Ritham, adjudicate disputes.

3. The situation

In October, Celia Jayamohan's customer-success team in Singapore matched July to September FASTag statements against trip records for 24 customer fleets (Exhibit 1). Of 612,000 transactions worth ₹9.60 crore, an analyst's rules flagged 8,160 for review. No claims have yet been filed from the flagged list. Celia reports that customer finance clerks often skip small claims because assembling the proof takes longer than the amount is worth. Her team assembled the audit by hand and closed it on Friday 9 October, nine days after the quarter ended.

Chinju's draft proposes software that spots mismatches inside the trip ledger and files the claim. It runs to 5,900 words, 31 user stories and seven appendix tables, and it covers dispute formats from four issuing banks. Engineering estimates five engineers for the 12 weeks of the build window, which runs 13 calendar weeks from 16 November to Friday 12 February 2027, less the year-end shutdown from Monday 28 December to Friday 1 January. That is 60 engineer-weeks of the squad's 84. One engineer's loaded cost is ₹33.6 lakh a year over 48 chargeable weeks, or ₹0.70 lakh per engineer-week, so the ask is ₹42 lakh.

Timing presses from outside. Ninety-six of the 410 customer contracts renew between December 2026 and March 2027, and a Dubai logistics client with Indian road operations renews on 30 November. Last quarter's committee, meeting on Monday 3 August, funded three of five proposals (Exhibit 2). Exhibit 3 places the dates against each other. The people involved will meet it from different places. The committee meeting falls at 12:30 in Singapore, 08:30 in Dubai, 05:30 in Berlin and 23:30 on Monday 2 November in New Jersey, because North American clocks go back on 1 November and Berlin's on 25 October.

The view differs by location. In Pune, the engineers who would build the feature asked for the bank formats to be stated before they would estimate, which the draft now does, and Cleetus has said he cannot staff a quarter on a promise he cannot restate in a sentence. In Edison, Cyril hears the toll question from shippers on renewal calls. In Singapore, Celia has seen how thin customers' records are. In Berlin, the studio lead has told Chinju that the prototype covers the happy path only.

4. The people

Chinju Jayasankar, senior product manager, Kochi, joined in 2023 and wrote the draft. She wants the feature funded without the squad being asked to carry unwritten promises.

Cleetus Jayaraj, vice-president of engineering, Pune, chairs the committee. He reads pre-reads on his phone, wants a clear boundary around the work, and needs to know what the squad will not be asked to build. He joined Ritham in 2021 and has chaired the committee since 2024.

Cyril Jayakrishnan, head of global sales, Edison, New Jersey, wants a written commitment he can take into the Dubai renewal on 30 November.

Celia Jayamohan, customer-success lead, Singapore, owns the audit. She wants customers' finance teams spared manual disputes and does not want the audit's flagged figures presented as money recovered. Her team would handle the first customers' questions if the feature ships.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: send the full draft. The 13 pages carry all 31 user stories, the four banks' dispute formats and the edge cases, so engineers can test the estimate against detail. Each committee member must read about 29.5 minutes for this one item, and Chinju needs roughly one more working day to finish the appendix tables.

Option B: send one page. A page of about 500 words, taking 2.5 minutes to read, states the problem, the proposal, why now and what the team will not do, with the draft linked as an appendix. It would take about two working days to write and to check against Cleetus, Celia and Cyril. Detail left off the page would have to be rebuilt at kick-off, and the page leaves the draft unread unless someone asks for it.

Option C: show the prototype. The Berlin studio built a clickable prototype in six days for ₹1.8 lakh, already paid. Chinju would ask for 20 minutes of the committee slot and send only a three-line note. The designer would join at 05:30 Berlin time. No written record would exist for Cyril to carry to Dubai, and the note would state no capacity ask.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What would the committee need from Chinju's proposal on 3 November, and which columns of Exhibit 2 bear on that?
  2. Exhibit 1 reports 8,160 flagged transactions. Which of its figures would you place under "problem", and which claims would they not support?
  3. Draft the "what we are not doing" list. Which items go on it, and who bears the cost of each?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what evidence arriving before 30 October would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

A one-pager is a decision tool before it is a document. Its four parts are the problem, the proposal, why now and what we are not doing, and the test is whether a reader can say what is being asked, and what is excluded, without opening anything else. Constraints do the work: a page cannot carry 31 user stories, so the writer must choose. The committee decides in a room, within a slot, among several proposals, so the writer's job is to make that choice easy to take and easy to defend afterwards.

A well-reasoned answer names the audience and the decision requested, uses figures that recompute from the evidence, separates what was measured from what is hoped, and states capacity in the committee's units.

One defensible path is Option B. The problem line would read: 8,160 of 612,000 transactions, ₹31.2 lakh of ₹960 lakh, flagged across 24 fleets in a quarter, unconfirmed. The proposal would start with wrong-class and duplicate deductions, 4,800 transactions and ₹21.3 lakh, or 68.3% of flagged value. Why now would cite the 96 renewals and the 30 November Dubai date. The not-doing line would list route-mismatch and "other" flags, and any promise of a recovery rate. The ask would be five engineers for 12 weeks, 60 of 84 engineer-weeks and ₹42 lakh. The draft and a prototype screenshot would sit behind links, and Cleetus and Celia would read the page before it is sent. Cyril would receive the same page, with a covering line that the squad's capacity, not a date, is what the committee is being asked to commit. In the room, the test is simple: if Cleetus can restate the request in one sentence and name two things the squad will not build, the page has done its work, and the first review after the squad starts on 16 November can open from the same sheet, so that scope is argued against a written line and not against memory.
exp40v2-req.one.pager:
Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Writing a one-pager

The smallest artefact in product management, the one with the highest ratio of consequence to word count, and the one about which competent practitioners most often disagree.

1Two rooms, one artefact

On Monday, 9 March 2026, Devika Nair had a blank document open and a deadline of Wednesday. She is a group product manager at Shailaja Health Cloud, a Chennai company that sells a laboratory information system — the software that runs a diagnostic laboratory's workflow from sample registration through analyser integration to report release. Shailaja has 210 customers, mostly regional lab chains of eight to sixty collection centres, and ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue. Thirty-one per cent of that revenue sits with eleven customers whose contracts renew between July and November.

The decision in front of her was whether to build a general health-data interoperability layer — a service that would let any Shailaja lab exchange structured reports with hospital systems, insurers and the national digital health infrastructure using standard clinical formats — or to keep doing what the company had been doing, which was building a bespoke integration each time a large customer demanded one. Eighteen bespoke integrations existed. Each had cost between ₹18 lakh and ₹40 lakh to build and consumed, in aggregate, about 1.4 engineers permanently in maintenance. Two of the eleven renewing customers had made interoperability an explicit condition of renewal. The general layer would cost, on the engineering director's rough estimate, nine engineer-quarters.

Devika's problem was not analytical. She had done the analysis. Her problem was that the investment committee met for ninety minutes on Friday, covered six items, and had never once, in her three years, changed a prior position on the strength of a verbal argument. Whatever she was going to persuade them of had to happen in a document read on Thursday evening by people she would not be in the room with when they read it.

Twelve hundred kilometres north, on the same Monday, Nikhil Barve was writing a different page for a different kind of company. Shailvi Bazaar is a Bengaluru marketplace for home and living goods — furnishings, lighting, kitchenware, a large handloom category — with 2.8 million monthly buyers and 46,000 active sellers, of whom about 5,400 are individual artisans or small workshops rather than trading companies. Nikhil's proposal concerned product photography. Analysis of the previous four quarters showed that listings with studio-grade images converted at 4.1% against 1.6% for listings with seller-shot images, and that the artisan segment — the segment whose supply the company's entire marketing position depended on — was overwhelmingly in the second group.

He wanted to fund a photography programme: assisted shoots in six cities, a guided in-app capture flow, and automated background replacement. The number that had been circulating internally was enormous, and Nikhil had begun to suspect it was wrong in the specific way that big numbers are usually wrong. He also suspected something more uncomfortable: that improving conversion for a few thousand artisan sellers while demand stayed flat would simply move orders from one set of sellers to another, and that the company would spend ₹3 crore to redistribute revenue rather than create it.

Two protagonists, two product types, one artefact. What follows is an argument about why that artefact is harder than it looks, what the best practitioners actually do with it, and where people who are genuinely good at this disagree with each other.

2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

A one-pager is a written argument, conventionally four hundred to seven hundred words, addressed to a named decider, asking for a single decision, and establishing four things: the problem as measured evidence; the proposal as a change in what somebody will be able to do; why now, as a claim about the world rather than about the author; and what is explicitly excluded. It differs from a product requirements document in audience and lifespan — the PRD is addressed to builders and lives as long as the feature does — and it differs from a strategy memo in scope, since a strategy memo argues about direction while a one-pager argues about a single allocation.

Its history runs through four traditions that are usually collapsed into one and should not be. Procter & Gamble institutionalised the one-page memo in the 1930s under Richard Deupree, and treated it as an instrument of managerial selection as much as communication: an executive who could not compress a recommendation to a page was thought not to have understood it. Barbara Minto, at McKinsey in the 1960s and 1970s, formalised the internal logic as the Pyramid Principle — answer first, then a small set of mutually exclusive supporting reasons, then evidence — which is a claim about the order in which arguments should be presented, not about their length. Amazon, from roughly 2004, moved in the opposite direction on length while doubling down on prose: Jeff Bezos banned slide presentations in favour of six-page narrative memos read in silence at the start of the meeting, and paired them with the PR/FAQ, a document written as a launch announcement for a product that does not yet exist. And the lean and continuous-discovery traditions — Steve Blank and Eric Ries in the late 2000s, Marty Cagan's writing on product teams, Teresa Torres's opportunity-solution trees in the 2010s — reframed the document as a hypothesis with a falsification condition rather than a proposal seeking approval.

These traditions share a diagnosis and disagree about the prescription. The shared diagnosis is that the expensive failure in organisations is not bad decisions but undeclared ones: the decision that was never framed, so nobody knows what was chosen or what was given up, and so nobody can tell six months later whether it worked. The disagreement is about how much apparatus is needed to prevent it.

Exhibit 1: five schools, and the specific proposition each would and would not sign.
SchoolWould signWould refuse to sign
P&G / one-page memo“If it does not fit on a page you have not decided what matters.”“Length should vary with the size of the bet.”
Minto / pyramid“The recommendation belongs in the first paragraph, before the evidence.”“Build the reader from problem to proposal in narrative order.”
Amazon narrative“Prose forces thought that bullets permit you to skip; read it in the room.”“One page is sufficient for a consequential decision.”
Lean / discovery“The page is a hypothesis and must name what would falsify it, by a date.”“A page can justify committing a quarter of engineering.”
Appetite / pitch“State the appetite — six weeks — not an estimate.”“Return-on-investment arithmetic on unbuilt software is meaningful.”

The columns are the useful part. Most practitioners can name the schools; far fewer can say which proposition they themselves would refuse to sign, which is the question that actually predicts how they will behave in a planning meeting.

Notice that the disagreements are not stylistic. The Amazon school and the P&G school differ on whether length should scale with consequence — a live question for Devika, whose decision commits nine engineer-quarters and touches contractual commitments. The lean school and the appetite school differ on whether the page should carry return-on-investment arithmetic at all, which determines whether Nikhil's central labour — getting the photography number right — is the heart of the work or an elaborate distraction. An expert holds a position on each of these and can say why.

3Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic that justifies the effort

Begin with a question that is rarely asked: what is a one-pager worth? It is answerable, and answering it disciplines everything downstream.

A document has value only insofar as it changes a decision. Let p be the probability that writing the document changes the outcome relative to what would have happened in an unstructured discussion; let Δ be the difference in value between the two outcomes; and let c be the cost of writing and reading it. The expected value of the document is p × Δ − c.

Apply this to Devika. The alternative to the general interoperability layer is eighteen months of further bespoke integrations: on trend, perhaps six more at an average ₹28 lakh, or ₹1.68 crore of build, plus a maintenance load growing from 1.4 to roughly 2.1 engineers, which at ₹60 lakh fully loaded per engineer-year over eighteen months is another ₹1.9 crore. Call the alternative path ₹3.6 crore of cost. The general layer costs nine engineer-quarters — 2.25 engineer-years, or ₹1.35 crore — plus a maintenance load she estimates at 0.6 engineers. The direct ₹Δ on cost alone is about ₹1.9 crore over eighteen months, before any revenue effect from the two renewals at risk, which between them represent ₹7.4 crore of ARR.

Now the probability. Devika's honest estimate is that without a written case, the committee defaults to the status quo roughly four times in five, because the status quo requires no one to sponsor it. With a well-made case she puts the odds of approval at perhaps 55%. So p, the incremental probability, is about 0.35. The document costs her two days — ₹50,000 of her time, plus perhaps ₹40,000 of committee reading time. The expected value is 0.35 × ₹1.9 crore − ₹0.9 lakh, which is roughly ₹66 lakh for two days of work. That ratio — three orders of magnitude — is why senior people who guard their time ferociously will still spend two days on six hundred words.

It also tells you when not to write one, which we return to in section four: when Δ is small, or when p is near zero because the decision has already been made politically and the document is ceremonial.

Expert practice has a sequence, and four of its steps are almost never written down. The first is naming the decision and the decider in a private sentence before drafting: I am asking the investment committee, on 13 March, to allocate nine engineer-quarters beginning 1 April. The second is writing the non-goals first, which sounds perverse and is the single most reliable accelerant available: the scope of a proposal is defined by its boundary, and authors who write the boundary first find the proposal paragraph almost writes itself. The third is pre-socialisation, discussed below, which determines the outcome more often than the prose does. The fourth is the cut ratio: strong practitioners routinely draft two to three times their target and delete, because generating then selecting produces better selection than trying to generate only what survives.

Now the second-order effects, which are where this topic stops being about writing and starts being about organisational behaviour. Three matter.

The first is legibility bias. When an organisation decides by document, proposals whose value is easy to quantify systematically beat proposals whose value is real but diffuse. Reliability work, developer productivity, accessibility, and the repayment of technical debt all lose to feature work in a one-pager culture, not because the deciders are foolish but because the artefact rewards a clean numerator. Mature organisations counteract this deliberately — by ring-fencing a share of capacity outside the committee process, or by requiring the committee to fund one proposal per cycle whose case is structural rather than numerical.

The second is a shift in who holds power. Deciding by document transfers influence from people who are quick and confident in a room to people who are careful on a page. This is usually an improvement in decision quality, and it is worth naming as a redistribution, because it produces predictable resistance from those who lose by it. It also has an equity dimension worth stating plainly: written decision-making advantages colleagues working in a second language less than fluent verbal debate does, and it advantages colleagues in other time zones enormously, which is why distributed organisations adopt it faster than co-located ones.

The third is proposal shaping. Once teams learn what kind of page gets approved, they begin generating proposals that fit it — three-month, single-team, cleanly measurable. The work that does not fit the container stops being proposed at all. An organisation can run for two years on well-argued one-pagers and discover it has made no decision larger than a quarter in that time.

4When the artefact applies, and when it actively misleads

The conditions can be stated as testable claims. Apply each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the resource is genuinely contested. If saying yes to this does not mean saying no to something else, the document has nothing to decide. True for Devika — nine engineer-quarters is a quarter of Shailaja's platform capacity. True for Nikhil, though less sharply, since the photography programme is mostly operational spend rather than engineering.

Claim two: the decision is consequential relative to the cost of reversing it. Jeff Bezos's distinction between one-way and two-way doors is the right instrument. Devika's is close to a one-way door: an interoperability layer becomes a contractual commitment to customers and is very hard to withdraw. Nikhil's is more reversible — a six-city pilot can be stopped — which is an argument for a shorter page and a faster decision, not for no page.

Claim three: the decider is not the author. The document's entire function is to carry an argument across a gap between minds. A one-pager written to yourself is a thinking tool, which is legitimate, but it should not be dressed as a decision document.

Claim four: evidence exists that can be honestly summarised. This is where Nikhil is on firmer ground than he thinks and Devika on shakier ground than she thinks: Nikhil has four quarters of conversion data on 46,000 sellers, while Devika's central claim — that interoperability determines renewal — rests on two customer conversations and a procurement questionnaire.

Claim five: the decision is not primarily a feasibility question. If the real uncertainty is whether the thing can be built at all, no amount of argument resolves it, and a two-week spike is worth more than any document. A page that asks for approval when the binding constraint is technical produces a confident yes to something that later turns out to be impossible, which is the worst available outcome.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. The first is ceremonial documentation: an organisation where the decision is made in advance and the page exists to create a record. Here p is near zero, the expected value is negative, and the rational response is to stop writing pages and start working out where decisions are actually made. The second is genuine novelty, where no relevant base rate exists and any numbers in the problem section would be invented; a prototype, a concierge test or a landing page beats a memo, and the honest one-pager in that situation asks for permission to run the test rather than to build the thing. The third is the very small and very reversible, where the document costs more than the decision is worth; teams that one-page everything develop an allergy to the format, and the allergy then costs them on the decisions that mattered.

5Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies. The question the format hides is whose profit-and-loss account improves. Shailaja Health Cloud sells a lab system and, separately, a radiology reporting product; the interoperability layer benefits both, which sounds like an advantage and functions in practice as an orphanage. Nobody's budget naturally carries a shared asset, and the page must therefore nominate an owner explicitly, including who pays for maintenance in year three when the original champion has moved on.

Two-sided marketplaces. Nikhil's case illustrates the sharpest version. A conversion improvement on the supply side, with demand held constant, can be pure redistribution: artisan listings win the sale that a trading-company listing would have won, gross merchandise value is unchanged, and the company has spent ₹3 crore to change who receives it. That may still be the right decision — if artisan supply is strategically scarce and the redistribution buys retention on the side that is hard to replace — but the page has to say so. The discipline for marketplace one-pagers is a sentence that most drafts omit: this proposal creates new transactions / redistributes existing transactions / does both, in roughly this proportion, and here is why we believe it.

Regulated products. In health, finance and insurance, a one-pager becomes a document of record, and anything asserted in it about clinical claims, patient-safety impact or regulatory compliance can be quoted back in an audit. Practitioners in these domains learn to separate the commercial argument from the regulatory claim, to state the compliance position as a question routed to a named reviewer rather than as a settled fact, and to avoid writing sentences like “this reduces diagnostic error” unless they are prepared to defend the evidence for it in a different kind of room.

Hardware plus software. Shaildhar Grid Systems, which makes rooftop solar inverters and the monitoring application that goes with them, operates on two clocks. Its one-pagers carry a section absent from pure software pages: the long-lead items — component qualification, tooling, safety certification, the factory build slot — and their calendar. The “why now” in a hardware page is frequently not a market claim but a manufacturing one: the next production run locks its bill of materials on a fixed date, and missing it costs not a quarter but a year.

AI-native products. This is where the classical template strains hardest. Shailrekha AI builds support agents that resolve customer queries end to end. Its proposals cannot promise a behaviour, only a distribution of behaviours, which breaks the convention that the proposal paragraph describes what a user will be able to do. Strong practice adapts in three ways: the problem section carries an evaluation baseline rather than only a business metric — current resolution rate 61% on a held-out set of 800 conversations, escalation-appropriateness 84%; the proposal states a target band with a confidence interval rather than a point; and the non-goals include quality floors, such as “we will not ship above a 2% rate of confidently wrong answers on billing queries, regardless of resolution gains.” The rise of this pattern is one of the few genuine changes to the artefact in twenty years.

The organisational seams. The hardest one-pagers are the ones whose proposal requires another team's quarter. A platform team's page that says “and the payments team will need to expose two new endpoints” is not a proposal; it is a request for a proposal that the payments team has not agreed to write. Mature companies handle this in a way they rarely describe in their process documentation: by the time the page circulates, the author has held five to eight one-to-one conversations, and the document is a recording of agreements already reached rather than an attempt to reach them. The meeting confirms; the corridor decides. Practitioners who learn the template but not the circuit write beautiful pages that die in committee, and conclude, wrongly, that their organisation does not value writing.

6Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The non-goals are a negotiation with the future, not a disclaimer

The tell-tale sign is what happens in week five. A competent practitioner writes non-goals that are true; an expert writes the ones that will be tested. When a vice-president asks in week five whether the interoperability layer could also handle insurance pre-authorisation, the author who wrote “not pre-authorisation, not claims” has a two-word answer and a document that a third party approved. The obvious reading — that non-goals clarify scope for the team — is too weak. Their real function is to create a prior commitment that survives seniority.

“Why now” is the section that decides, and the section most often faked

An expert reads the why-now section first, because it is the only one that distinguishes this quarter from any other and therefore the only one that engages with the actual scarcity. The tell is a why-now that would have been equally true a year ago. Devika's first draft said “interoperability is increasingly important”, which was true in 2023 and will be true in 2029. Her second said “two renewals worth ₹7.4 crore close between July and September and both have interoperability in their procurement checklist”, which is a claim with a date attached and can be checked.

Numbers must survive one round of division

The expert's instinct on seeing a large round number is not admiration but division: by the denominator, by the time period, and by the conversion from a gross flow to a margin. Nikhil's circulating number — “a 2.5-point conversion gap across 5,400 artisan sellers is worth ₹60 crore of GMV” — collapses under two divisions, first to the take rate and then to the share of the gap that better photographs can actually close. The obvious reading is that big numbers make a strong case. In a room of experienced people, an undivided big number makes a weak one, because it signals that the author has not yet done the work.

The document's real audience is the person who reads it without you

Every page has two readers: the colleagues who were pre-socialised and will read charitably, and the finance director three levels away reading at 11 p.m. who has never met the team. Experts write for the second reader, which is why they include denominators, date ranges and sources that feel unnecessary to the first. The tell of a page written only for the first reader is the unexplained internal name — a project codename, a system, a metric defined nowhere.

An estimate in a one-pager becomes a commitment, whatever the disclaimer says

“Roughly nine engineer-quarters” will be quoted back as nine engineer-quarters in September. Experts either give a band with an explicit confidence statement (“seven to twelve, and I will know which by the end of April”) or adopt the appetite framing and state a fixed budget with variable scope (“one quarter, one team, and we will ship whatever subset is coherent”). What they do not do is write a point estimate and hope the word “roughly” protects them.

Writing it is a discovery instrument, not only a communication one

The most common experience among strong writers is that they change their own mind during the third paragraph. Devika began believing the case was about engineering cost and finished believing it was about renewal risk, which is a different proposal with a different sponsor. The tell that someone is using the page only as communication is that the draft never changed its conclusion — a document that arrived at exactly the position the author held before writing is, more often than not, a document that did no thinking.

Length should track irreversibility, not importance

This is the most useful reconciliation of the one-page and six-page schools. Importance is the wrong variable, because important-but-reversible decisions should be made fast and revisited. Irreversibility is the right one. Nikhil's pilot is reversible and deserves a short page and a quick answer; Devika's layer is a contractual commitment to 210 customers and arguably deserves four pages and a fortnight. Experts scale the artefact to the door, not to the budget.

The cheapest quality test is the one-sentence retelling

Hand the page to someone uninvolved, wait an hour, and ask what it proposed and what it excluded. If they can produce both in one sentence each, the page works. If they retell the background instead, the page is a briefing wearing a proposal's clothes. Experts run this test before circulation; competent practitioners discover the answer in the meeting.

A one-pager cannot tell you whether your organisation can execute

This is the limit of the artefact however well it is written. It can establish that a thing is worth doing and not establish that this team, with these dependencies, in this quarter, will do it. The expert's habit is to read the last three approved one-pagers alongside what actually shipped, and to apply the resulting correction factor privately to every new page, including their own. An organisation that has never done this comparison is deciding on arguments with no feedback loop, which over a few years produces confident and systematically optimistic committees.

7What genuinely varies by product type and stage

Some of the received wisdom about product-type differences is real and some is decoration. The real differences are these.

In consumer products the evidence base is behavioural and abundant, so the binding constraint is honesty about causation rather than availability of data; the characteristic failure is a correlation presented as a mechanism. In B2B and enterprise, the buyer and the user are different people, so the problem section must complete a chain from user pain to a metric the buyer is measured on, and “why now” is usually a contractual or regulatory date rather than a market movement. In platforms and marketplaces, the page must name the side and must distinguish creation from redistribution, as discussed. In hardware, the calendar section is load-bearing and the reversibility calculus changes completely, because a bill of materials locked in March cannot be reconsidered in June. In AI products, the proposal is a distribution rather than a behaviour, and the non-goals must include quality floors.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly, because a great deal of ink is spilled on it. The four sections do not change. The requirement for a named decider does not change. The need for a falsifiable check does not change. The claim, sometimes heard, that enterprise products need longer documents because enterprise customers are complicated confuses the specification with the argument: the specification is indeed longer, and it is not a one-pager.

Stage changes the document's function more than its form. In a company of twelve, the page is usually addressed to a founder in the same room, and its real job is to slow a decision that would otherwise be made in ninety seconds in a corridor; the useful section is often the non-goals, because the founder's instinct is to say yes to everything. Between about fifty and three hundred people, the one-pager becomes the mechanism by which the organisation learns that decisions have costs, and this is the stage at which introducing it changes behaviour most. Above a thousand, the page must travel without its author across functions and time zones, and the discipline shifts to self-containment: every number sourced, every internal name expanded, every dependency named as a person and a date.

8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Devika's page, reworked. Her first draft led with the engineering-cost argument: eighteen bespoke integrations, ₹28 lakh average, 1.4 engineers of permanent maintenance, growing. The arithmetic was sound — ₹3.6 crore over eighteen months on the status-quo path against ₹1.35 crore of build plus 0.6 engineers of maintenance — and it was, as an argument to an investment committee, merely adequate, because cost avoidance always competes badly against revenue. Her second draft led with renewal: ₹7.4 crore of ARR in two accounts with interoperability in the procurement checklist, against ₹96 crore total ARR, in a renewal window that opens in July. The engineering-cost case moved to the third paragraph, where it functioned as reinforcement. Same evidence, same recommendation, a different load-bearing claim — and the honest caveat she added was that two customer conversations do not establish that interoperability determines renewal, so the page proposed a four-week pre-commitment: ask all eleven renewing accounts directly, before locking the April start.

Nikhil's page, and the division that changed it. The circulating number was ₹60 crore of GMV. Here is the arithmetic done properly. Artisan listings generate roughly ₹340 crore of annual GMV. Closing a 2.5-point conversion gap from 1.6% to 4.1% would, taken naively, more than double it. But the first division is the take rate — Shailvi Bazaar earns 11% — which converts ₹60 crore of incremental GMV into ₹6.6 crore of revenue. The second division is attribution: studio photography is correlated with sellers who are also better at pricing, titling and fulfilment, and Nikhil's matched-pair analysis on 1,100 listings suggested photography alone accounted for about 40% of the observed gap. That is ₹2.6 crore. The third division is the one almost nobody does: of the incremental orders, his marketplace-economics colleague estimated that 55% would come from demand that would otherwise have gone to trading-company listings on the same platform — redistribution, not creation. The genuinely incremental revenue is about ₹1.2 crore a year against a programme cost of ₹3 crore in year one and ₹1.1 crore recurring.

That arithmetic does not kill the proposal; it changes it. The revenue case alone does not clear the cost, so if the page were to rest on revenue it should be rejected. The case that survives is a supply-retention case: artisan sellers who make fewer than two sales a month churn off the platform at 47% within six months, and artisan supply is the reason Shailvi Bazaar can charge what it charges.
