The programme he originally wanted became the thing the page says it is not doing.

The failure: Shailendra Freight Systems. In 2024 a product manager at this Pune truck-matching platform wrote a one-pager that won approval and should not have. The problem section was excellent: 23% of confirmed loads were cancelled by the fleet owner after acceptance, measured over six months across 41,000 bookings, with a clean cost per cancellation of ₹1,840 in support handling and re-matching. The proposal — a commitment score shown to shippers and a penalty regime for repeat cancellers — was clear. The why-now was honest. What the page did not contain was a single non-goal, and the omission was not cosmetic.

Within five weeks, four things had been added: an appeals process for penalised fleet owners, because the supply team correctly pointed out that penalising scarce supply without recourse was dangerous; an integration with two telematics providers to verify the reasons given for cancellation; a revised score for shippers as well, on the argument of symmetry; and a rollback mechanism. The quarter's work became two quarters and a week. Worse, the penalty regime went live before the appeals process was finished, roughly 900 fleet owners were downgraded on unverified reasons, and 130 of them stopped taking loads on the platform altogether during the festive peak — the single worst four weeks of the year to lose supply.

The recovery is instructive because it was not a rewrite. The company suspended penalties within eleven days, kept the score as a display-only signal, and personally called the 130 fleet owners; 84 returned. Then the head of product changed the template: every one-pager at Shailendra Freight Systems now requires a section headed “what we will not build, and who will be unhappy about each”, with a named person per line. It is a slightly humiliating section to write and it has, by the company's own reckoning, prevented two comparable episodes. The lesson is not that non-goals are good hygiene. It is that non-goals are a risk control, and a page without them transfers scope decisions to whoever raises them loudest in week five.

9Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

The undivided number. The early warning is a figure that is large, round and appears before any denominator. The diagnostic question takes eight seconds: what is that divided by, and over what period? Caught at draft stage it costs an afternoon of analysis. Caught in the meeting it costs the author's credibility for two quarters. Caught after the build, it costs the project, since a feature justified by a number that turns out to be inflated is the easiest thing in any organisation to cancel.

The absent non-goals. The early warning is that nobody objected in the meeting. Objection is information; its total absence usually means the proposal was so unbounded that everyone could read their own preference into it. The diagnostic is to ask at the end of the meeting what was just declined and count how many people can answer. Caught late, this is the Shailendra failure, costing a quarter of schedule and, in that case, a festive peak.

The ceremonial page. The early warning is that comments arrive only after the decision, and only on wording. The diagnostic question is the uncomfortable one: has a proposal in this forum ever been rejected, or materially changed, on the strength of the document? If the honest answer is no, the cost of not noticing is every hour spent writing pages for two years.

The feasibility-shaped hole. The early warning is an engineering estimate expressed as a single number with no band, offered quickly. The diagnostic is to ask the engineer what they would need to see to be confident within twenty per cent, and how long that would take. Caught at draft, it costs a two-week spike. Caught in month three, it costs the difference between the estimate and reality, which in the cases that matter is a multiple rather than a margin.

Metric drift after approval. The early warning is a progress update that reports a different measure from the one the page named. The diagnostic is to reread the page's check at every review, out loud. Caught late, the project becomes unfalsifiable and can only end through exhaustion or reorganisation — which is how most doomed projects actually end.

The page that decided nothing. The early warning is an approval with no resource attached: “yes, let's do it, work out the capacity with the platform team.” The diagnostic is to ask, before leaving the room, who is now assigned and from when. Caught late, the author spends a quarter negotiating for people while believing they have a mandate.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

One page or six. The one-page position, in its strongest form, holds that the constraint is the mechanism: length is unbounded and therefore length expands to fill available anxiety, and only a hard limit forces the selection that constitutes thinking. Its evidence is decades of P&G practice and the observable fact that longer documents receive less careful reading per word. The six-page position holds that this confuses brevity with compression — that a page forces omission of genuine complexity and that the resulting decisions are confident and under-informed; its evidence is Amazon's sustained use of narrative memos for exactly the decisions that matter most. For the one-page position to be wrong, it would have to be true that consequential decisions routinely fail for want of context that would have fitted in five more pages. For the six-page position to be wrong, it would have to be true that the extra pages are not actually read, which is an empirical question about your own organisation that you can answer by asking three readers what page four said.

Return-on-investment arithmetic versus appetite. The arithmetic school holds that any resource request must state its expected return, because otherwise allocation degenerates into advocacy and seniority. The appetite school — associated with the Basecamp pitch tradition — holds that ROI numbers on unbuilt software are elaborate fiction, that the honest unit of decision is how much time the thing is worth rather than what it will return, and that fixing the budget and varying the scope produces better outcomes than fixing the scope and varying the budget. The appetite position is strongest for exploratory work where no base rate exists. It is weakest where a real base rate does exist — Nikhil has four quarters of conversion data on 46,000 sellers, and refusing to do the arithmetic there would be a choice not to know.

Whether the page should commit resources or only commit to discovery. The discovery school says a one-pager should never authorise a quarter of building; it should authorise a two-week test whose results authorise the next step. Against this stands the observation that some investments are not testable in small pieces — Devika's interoperability layer either exists or does not — and that an organisation which can only commit two weeks at a time cannot build infrastructure. The steelman of the discovery position is that most things claimed to be indivisible are divisible by someone willing to think harder about sequencing; the steelman of the other is that the cost of over-decomposing a genuinely coherent system is paid in integration complexity that nobody counts.

Who owns the non-goals. One camp holds that the author declares them, because the author has thought hardest about scope. The other holds that non-goals are precisely what the decider is deciding, and that an author who declares them is quietly removing options from the decision. In practice, mature organisations split the difference: the author proposes non-goals and the minutes record which ones the decider adopted, because a non-goal the decider never noticed provides no protection in week five.

Whether a drafted-by-machine one-pager still does its job. This is the live disagreement, and it is unresolved. One position holds that the artefact's value was always the thinking that writing forces, so a page generated from a prompt is a page nobody thought through, and the fluency of the output actively disguises the absence. The other holds that this romanticises drafting: generation was never the hard part, selection was, and a tool that produces a competent draft in four minutes lets the author spend their two days on the division of the numbers and the circuit of conversations that actually determine the outcome. Both positions have adherents who write well. What would settle it is evidence about whether authors who draft with assistance change their own minds during the process at the same rate as those who do not — the third-paragraph reversal described above — and no one has that evidence yet.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the format produces a page with four correct headings. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They spend most of their time outside the document. The two days allocated to a one-pager are, for an expert, roughly four hours of writing and twelve of conversation and arithmetic, because they know that the page records a position reached elsewhere. They write the non-goals before the proposal, because the boundary defines the thing. They divide every number before it goes on the page, and they can state the denominator of each from memory. And they treat the page as falsifiable: they name a check and a date, and they return to it, which means they accumulate a personal record of how often their arguments were right — a record that, over five years, is worth more than any framework.

There is a fifth sign, subtler and more reliable than the others. An expert can be talked out of their own proposal in the pre-read and does not experience this as a loss. The page exists to reach a good decision, not to win; someone who has internalised that will occasionally circulate a document whose recommendation is do not do this, and here is what I believed a week ago and why I no longer believe it. Committees that receive such a document twice from the same author begin to read everything that author writes differently, which is the closest thing to durable influence that a written culture offers.

12What each protagonist decided

Devika circulated 680 words on the Wednesday evening with a two-page technical appendix marked optional. She led with the renewal exposure, kept the engineering-cost argument as reinforcement, and named her weakest claim explicitly: that two conversations do not establish a pattern. Her proposal was therefore conditional — four weeks of structured conversations with all eleven renewing accounts, then a go or no-go on 15 April with the nine engineer-quarters pre-reserved but not committed. The committee approved the conditional structure in four minutes. She had asked for a smaller, better-shaped yes than her first draft would have sought, and she got it without spending anybody's credibility.

Nikhil did something harder. He deleted the programme he had wanted for six months and wrote a page proposing the ₹70 lakh two-city pilot with a supply-retention metric, with the national rollout listed under what we are not doing. The sentence he found most difficult to write was the honest one about cannibalisation, because it undercut the number his own leadership had been quoting in reviews. He wrote it anyway, and added the line that in his judgement made the page credible: if the retention effect is real, the revenue case follows in year two; if I am wrong about retention, this pilot will tell us for ₹70 lakh rather than ₹3 crore.

Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Devika's conditional proposal is safer than an outright request, but pre-reserving nine engineer-quarters for four weeks has a cost that her page does not quantify — what is it, who bears it, and should it have been on the page? Second: Nikhil's cannibalisation estimate of 55% is, by his own admission, the weakest number in his analysis, yet it is the number that reduces the case from ₹2.6 crore to ₹1.2 crore — is it defensible to let the weakest input carry the most decisive division, and what would you have done instead? Third: the Shailendra Freight Systems template now requires a named unhappy person beside each non-goal — what does that practice cost the organisation over five years, and under what conditions would you remove it?

13Going deeper

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc. The one-pager is the smallest member of a family, and most confusion about it comes from importing the habits of a larger sibling; knowing which artefact answers which question prevents the commonest failure, which is a one-pager full of acceptance criteria and empty of argument.

Writing clearly. The skill this entire artefact rests on: with only six hundred words available, every vague sentence is expensive, and the habits that make a sentence carry weight are learnable independently of any template.

PRD structure. What you earn the right to write when the one-pager wins; it fails in the opposite direction — not by being too long but by being too vague at the edges — and learning both teaches you which register a given reader needs.

Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N). The technique that rescues a proposal paragraph from feature-listing, by forcing you to describe a named person's first day and hundredth day with the thing; it is also the fastest way to discover that a proposal has no coherent user.

Acceptance criteria and error cases. Where the non-goals of a one-pager become concrete and testable; the discipline of enumerating what should happen when things go wrong is the bridge from argument to buildable specification.

Telemetry requirements. The check named in a one-pager is only real if the data exists to evaluate it; teams that specify telemetry alongside the proposal can answer the six-month question, and teams that do not end projects by exhaustion.

Non-functional requirements. Latency, reliability, privacy and accessibility are the constraints most often missing from a one-pager and most expensive to add in month three, particularly in regulated and AI-native products where they are not negotiable.

Release criteria and success metrics. The other end of the same argument: the one-pager makes a falsifiable claim, and release criteria are where that claim is finally tested against reality rather than against a committee.
